key_insight: KAISEN shows that subgroup fairness audits for clinical risk models are only reliable when each step is stress-tested, because significance, mitigation, diagnostics, and drift monitoring can all behave very differently under known ground truth.
engineering_relevance: For deployed clinical ML systems, the paper argues that audit outputs should report subgroup-specific variability, detectable-effect floors, and transfer risk across cohorts rather than a single aggregate fairness score.
method: Five-phase reproducible audit pipeline: stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, mitigation, and drift monitoring.
Evaluated on a synthetic benchmark with 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes, and three subgroup intersections.
Stress-tested each component against known ground truth to probe where the audit succeeds or fails.
evidence_signal: Across 48 held-out runs, group-wise threshold optimization reduced equalized-odds disparity in every run, while group-wise Platt scaling improved it in only 19 of 48; the diagnostic also failed on all 48 model-driven proxy-misspecification cases.
watch_item: Results are fully synthetic, so the pipeline’s apparent performance and failure modes may not transfer to real clinical data without further validation.
paper_title: KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models
